citations.quote: The QuickSAT/Xen Space Hypervisor is a hypervisor environment for space vehicles with initial implementation targeted at BUSAT and EarthScan CubeSAT
It is currently in use on the University NanoSat Program, at AFRL and at NASA research centers.
QuickSAT/step_SATdb, is a collaborative, "push button" design and manufacturing environment for satellite manufacturers, government agencies and universities.

The design, payload definition and manufacturing process requires currently a wide range of design and management tools that have limited consistency, data interchange capability, and a lack of coherency within the aerospace industry and particularly the satellite development community. Beginning in the late 1990's the Space Industry began an effort to streamline this process to pursue the capability to assemble, test and launch a satellite within months and sometimes days, versus years, of a customer's request. The effort began with defining a standard for "Plug and Play" parts, and a method for attaching components, cables and networks in a satellite for ease of design, assembly and manufacturing. A need existed however to detail the relationships between the satellite configuration (components, payloads and interrelationships), manage inventories, provide for life cycle management, design, analysis and test data, and to automate the design and manufacturing process.

step_SATdb seamlessly integrates existing detail design tools with QuickSAT, as well as databases tracking requirements, hardware and software components and parts in inventory, along with the final configuration of the satellite. QuickSAT provides for rapid design and coherency between a range of applications and data sets. step_SATdb stores and distributes supporting satellite design, configuration, mission, support and test data from a centralized database and can distribute the data across multiple platforms and via the internet and proprietary networks.
Power modeling - both systems level and detail based on modes of flight for each flight leg.
Modes of operation can define which systems and payloads are in use for a given mode.

With QuickSAT/step_SATdb you can save multiple configurations of a given satellite model and flight plan and compare the models, design and analytics results. Designs are fully traceable and you can baseline a mission or alternative flight plans from prior projects. Payloads and their software can be modified, however prior versions are stored to maintain fully traceable models and designs. Payloads can be easily swapped out in QuickSAT.

Currently, several clouds are active, one of which, www.quick-sat.com, serves NASA, SAIC, government subcontractors and the University Nanosat Community, plus others who support satellite development.

Through QuickSAT, the user can then define the mission flight plan and modes of operation, defining which elements of the satellite are operational for each mode of flight, covering mass, power and volume.

Using the flight plan and mode information, the user can define a schedule of which modes are operational based on conditions, or events, for a given flight leg through the QuickSAT/Scheduler. For example defining the conditions to turn on an imager, when to transmit data or when to go into a safe hold mode. Using this knowledge we can define an event driven schedule and model and simulate other factors such as power utilization throughout a mission or propellants used.

This schedule of conditions along with payload software models and applications are downloaded from QuickSAT to the vehicle on board processor and the Xen Hypervisor including. The hypervisor then creates and operates the virtualized payloads, providing all the security, robustness and performance expected from an ARINC 653 based hypervisor.

In order to manage the start/stop/operation of various virtualized payloads and related processes, the SQL database, called the Mission Flight Plan and populated by QuickSAT/VMS, is read by the QuickSAT/Xen- Scheduler. The Mission Flight Plan file defines all available flight conditions, and the functions to be acted once the condition has been met. All conditions are monitored via the Condition Handler.
The second element of the QuickSAT/Xen-Scheduler is the System Controller that acts on the conditions once they occur per the Condition Handler.

Through QuickSAT/Designer the user defines: the satellite configuration, parameter information - the parameter ID and name, parameter type, conversion factor, and units - and where the parameter can be found and how the data is sent and received (Ethernet, space wire, serial bus ID, etc). All of this is referred to as the Satellite Data Model (SDM).

The SDM is then transferred from a local device (computer or laptop) to the flight hardware via the QuickSAT/Satellite Management Tool. Once loaded on the flight hardware QuickSAT/Xen-Scheduler knows where to find and send the data.

Modes of operation define what systems and payloads are to be used for a give mode; this also defines which related software modules are used and in turn defines the operation of a virtualized payload. Figure 8 shows the Mode Modeling Screen used within QuickSAT. Using this knowledge we can define an event driven schedule and model and simulate other factors such as power utilization throughout a mission or propellants used. As shown in Figure 5, the QuickSAT/scheduler will generate a file called the Mission Plan File that captures the defined mission schedule.

QuickSAT/Designer is not only a satellite modeling and definition tool, but also defines all components used within a satellite - hardware, mechanical components and software. From this we can define a complete satellite configuration (including location, mass, volume, moments of inertia, and orientation), the software parameters for a given component, and how it is networked to the data architecture. This complete model defines the Satellite Data Model.

Combining QuickSAT with the space hypervisor environment we can rapidly model our virtualized payloads and supporting mission plan. Definitions can be reconfigured and new models generated. Most importantly, QuickSAT retains all prior models and configurations - designs can be traced and prior models can be used, plus comparative studies can be done.

Testing will be done utilizing a BeagleBone Black board, the same system used for the BUSAT Mission. Once developed, the software rad-hardening tools will be tested using real applications running on virtual machines on the BUSAT Mission including the C&CH module, the communications module, and the ADCS module. Testing will be conducted in a lab setting, through ground based testing, high altitude balloon flights and the BUSAT Mission in low Earth orbit. At the conclusion of this program software based rad-hardening system will be flight qualified.

However if DOM0 (the master domain) experiences a failure from an SEU, the system will still fail. To alleviate this problem the sci Zone team is also developing the HAL-M manager (Figure 4), an application that will manage multiple "DOM0s" and maintain consistency between them and restart any failed DOM0.

Now, small satellite programs, such as nanosat and cubesat projects, have an open source hypervisor and software environment to define virtual processes and payloads, define their application, and rapidly define conditions for their use without the need of a large size software staff.
Santangelo, Andrew, "QuickSAT/step_SATdb: A Satellite Concurrent Design Automation and Design for Manufacturability cloud based environment for Responsive Space", AIAA-2426, September 28, 2011.
